speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I understand you are an 8-month-old boy experiencing feeding difficulties and abdominal distension. To help me understand your condition better, do you or your parents notice any episodes of severe, intermittent crying or drawing your legs up to your chest?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: That pain on touch and fussy behavior is concerning; have you noticed any episodes of bilious (green) vomiting or "currant jelly" stools? REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_Ultrasound.

speaker: Doctor
text: I see the ultrasound results are listed as "normal readings," which is unusual given your symptoms. Have you noticed if the stool looks like red currant jelly or contains blood? Also, have you passed any stool since the feeding difficulties started?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: I understand there has been no fever, vomiting, or diarrhea, and the baby had an uncomplicated full-term birth; given the normal ultrasound and lack of "currant jelly" stools so far, does the baby have a history of constipation or does the abdomen feel hard and tender to the touch? REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal_X-Ray.

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal_X-Ray. The history of obstipation (lack of stool) combined with progressive abdominal distension and decreased feeding suggests a mechanical obstruction; please provide the radiograph to look for the "double bubble" sign or other signs of distal obstruction.

speaker: Patient
text: The abdomen still looks swollen and the baby seems uncomfortable, especially in the lower abdomen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis

**Correction Note:** Upon re-evaluating the clinical picture in an 8-month-old (typical onset for intussusception is 6-36 months, but pyloric stenosis peaks at 5-6 weeks; however, the "normal" ultrasound rules out pyloric stenosis as the primary cause of current obstruction). Given the age (8 months), symptoms of feeding difficulty, abdominal distension, obstipation (no stool), and a normal abdominal ultrasound (which effectively rules out pyloric stenosis and large masses), the most likely diagnosis is **Intussusception** (even without classic "currant jelly" stool yet) or **Distal Intestinal Obstruction** (e.g., Meconium Ileus or Malrotation). The "normal ultrasound" is a critical negative finding that makes pyloric stenosis impossible.
